extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning mathematical/propositional (sentential) logic
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter teaching the syntax and semantics of sentential (propositional) logic: defining symbols and well-formed formulas, construction sequences and induction, truth assignments and truth-table methods, basic tautologies, parsing algorithm, and related theorems (e.g., compactness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part description of a formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal language description should (1) specify the set of symbols (the alphabet), (2) specify the rules for forming the 'grammatically correct' finite sequences of symbols (well-formed formulas, wffs), and (3) indicate the allowable translations between English and the formal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the third part assigns any meaning to wffs; the first two parts suffice for purely syntactic manipulation. Examples given: symbols (, ), →, ¬, A1, A2, ...; example wff (A1 → (¬ A2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formula (wff) formation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Wffs are defined by: (a) every sentence symbol is a wff; (b) if α and β are wffs then (¬ α), (α ∧ β), (α ∨ β), (α → β), and (α ↔ β) are wffs; (c) no expression is a wff unless compelled by (a) and (b). Equivalently, via formula-building operations E¬, E∧, E∨, E→, E↔.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empty sequence is not a wff. Examples show building complex wffs by finite applications of the operations. The explicit equations E¬(α)=(¬ α), E∧(α,β)=(α ∧ β), etc., are given to formalize construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction sequences and structural induction principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A construction sequence is a finite sequence of expressions where each term is either a sentence symbol or obtained by applying a formula-building operation to earlier terms. The induction principle: if S is a set of wffs containing all sentence symbols and closed under the five formula-building operations, then S is the set of all wffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use construction sequences (or ancestral trees) to argue properties of all wffs by induction. Examples and exercises demonstrate using this principle to prove combinatorial facts about lengths, counts of connective/sentence-symbol occurrences, and uniqueness of extensions of truth assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol assumptions for unique decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an infinite sequence of distinct symbols (A1, A2, ...) and that no symbol is a finite sequence of other symbols (i.e., each listed symbol is atomic and not concatenation of symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents ambiguity and ensures finite sequences of symbols are uniquely decomposable (if a1...am = b1...bn with each ai, bj a symbol then m=n and ai=bi). The assumption is highlighted as important for unique parsing and later results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced parentheses and initial-segment property
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff has the same number of left and right parentheses (balanced), and any proper initial segment of a wff contains an excess of left parentheses (no proper initial segment can itself be a wff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 13A and 13B support uniqueness of decomposition and parsing; proofs use the induction principle. Use this to show why parentheses eliminate ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of truth assignments and extension to wffs (semantic clauses 0–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth assignment v for a set S of sentence symbols is a function v:S→{F,T}. There is a unique extension v to all wffs built from S satisfying: 0) v(A)=v(A) for A∈S; 1) v((¬ α)) = T iff v(α)=F; 2) v((α ∧ β)) = T iff v(α)=T and v(β)=T; 3) v((α ∨ β)) = T iff v(α)=T or v(β)=T (or both); 4) v((α → β)) = F iff v(α)=T and v(β)=F (conditional is vacuously true when antecedent false); 5) v((α ↔ β)) = T iff v(α)=v(β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table III gives the truth values in tabular form. This clause-by-clause semantic definition is used to compute truth values by working up the construction tree; vacuous truth of → is emphasized with everyday-language cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation by construction tree (bottom-up computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute v(ϕ) for a complex wff ϕ given v on sentence symbols, form the ancestral (construction) tree of ϕ and assign truth values to each vertex from the leaves upward using the semantic clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: compute v for ((A2 → (A1 → A6)) ↔ ((A2 ∧ A1) → A6)) by evaluating subexpressions in order. The tree method compresses computation and makes uniqueness of evaluation clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tautological implication and tautology (semantic entailment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a set Γ of wffs and a wff τ, Γ tautologically implies τ (Γ |= τ) iff every truth assignment for the sentence symbols in Γ ∪ {τ} that satisfies every member of Γ also satisfies τ. τ is a tautology (|= τ) if ∅ |= τ (i.e., every truth assignment satisfies τ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases: if Γ is unsatisfiable then Γ |= τ vacuously for every τ; empty-premise entailment corresponds to tautologies. Examples: {A,(A→B)}|=B; equivalence and mutual entailment definitions (σ |= τ and τ |= σ give tautological equivalence σ |==| τ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-table method for checking entailment and tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given wffs σ1,...,σk and τ over n sentence symbols, construct the truth table with 2^n rows enumerating all truth assignments and compute values of each formula to check whether every row that satisfies all σi also satisfies τ (or to check if a single formula is a tautology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure illustrated with examples. Practical guidance: exploit symmetry or short-circuit cases to reduce rows (e.g., handle cases where a connective's truth is fixed by one symbol). Complexity note: full truth tables require 2^n rows; exponential growth makes the method impractical for large n and motivates search for more efficient theorem-proving methods (P vs NP remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness theorem (semantic compactness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is an infinite set of wffs such that every finite subset Γ0 of Γ is satisfiable (there is a truth assignment satisfying every member of Γ0), then Γ itself is satisfiable (there is a truth assignment satisfying every member of Γ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restatement: if every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable then Γ is satisfiable. Remark: relates to compactness in topology (product space) and can be proved via Tychonoff's theorem; this is flagged as a significant nontrivial fact to be proved later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected basic tautologies and logical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful and commonly used tautologies include associative and commutative laws for ∧, ∨, ↔; distributive laws ((A ∧ (B ∨ C)) ↔ ((A ∧ B) ∨ (A ∧ C))) and its dual; negation identities ((¬ (¬ A)) ↔ A), ((¬ (A → B)) ↔ (A ∧ (¬ B))), and other De Morgan laws; excluded middle (A ∨ (¬ A)), contradiction (¬ (A ∧ (¬ A))), contraposition ((A → B) ↔ ((¬ B) → (¬ A))), exportation (((A ∧ B) → C) ↔ (A → (B → C))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provide algebraic/manipulative identities used in proofs and transformations. The text lists them as a 'Selected List of Tautologies' with examples to use for substitution and equivalence manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution principle (preservation of tautologies)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is a tautology then any formula ϕ* obtained by uniformly replacing each sentence symbol An by an arbitrary wff αn is also a tautology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: formalize substitution and show: if v is a truth assignment then define u(An)=v(αn) to relate evaluations; use induction principle. Example: from ((A ∧ B) ↔ (B ∧ A)) conclude ((α ∧ β) ↔ (β ∧ α)) is a tautology for arbitrary α, β.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality principle for ∧, ∨, ¬
rubrics_metrics.description: For a wff α whose only connectives are ∧, ∨, and ¬, define α* by interchanging ∧ and ∨ and replacing each sentence symbol by its negation. Then α* is tautologically equivalent to (¬ α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the induction principle to prove. Consequence: if α |==| β then α* |==| β* (duality preserves equivalence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing algorithm and uniqueness of parse tree
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit four-step parsing algorithm: (1) if all minimal vertices are sentence symbols halt (tree built); otherwise select a minimal non-sentence expression; (2) first symbol must be '(' (otherwise reject); (3) if second symbol not '¬', scan left to find first balanced prefix α — that is the left constituent; next symbol is principal binary connective and remainder β) is the right constituent; create left/right child nodes and repeat; (4) if second symbol is '¬', take remainder β) as single child and repeat. The algorithm halts and constructs a unique tree if the expression is a wff; otherwise rejects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctness comments: halting follows because vertex expressions strictly shorten; choices in step 3 are forced by balance/initial-segment lemmas so the parse is unique. Rejection criteria: missing expected parentheses, failure to find balanced prefix, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing consequences for ambiguity and parentheses usage
rubrics_metrics.description: With the given parenthesized notation every wff is formed in a unique way (unique decomposition) so parentheses eliminate ambiguity; lacking parentheses would create ambiguous parses (e.g., A1 ∨ A2 ∧ A3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text motivates parentheses by showing ambiguity without them and proves uniqueness via the parsing algorithm and earlier lemmas. Practical implication: the syntactic rules plus parentheses guarantee deterministic tree construction and unique evaluation.
